lead: Every project must do the same SDLC phases: requirements, design, build, test. A process model decides the order, how often each phase repeats, and when the user first sees working software. Waterfall runs the phases once, in sequence. Incremental runs them once per slice of the product. Spiral runs them in repeated loops, and each loop starts with an explicit risk analysis. The choice turns on two questions: how stable the requirements are, and how much risk the project carries. A fixed-scope tax system and a new consumer app need different answers.
prereq: You need: 1.3 for the SDLC phases and 1.4 for what a process model is.

sections.h3: Waterfall: one pass, documents at every step

blocks.text: In the waterfall model the phases run one after another, once. Requirements end before design begins, design ends before coding begins, coding ends before testing begins. Each phase closes with a written document (a requirements specification, a design document, a test plan) that the next phase works from. The model is document-driven: paper, not conversation, carries the work forward.

This suits work where the requirement is already fixed and must be provable: a statutory report, a payroll layout set by law, a contract with fixed price and fixed scope. The documents also create review gates, which safety-critical projects want.

items: The user runs working software only near the end, so a misread requirement surfaces at test time, when fixing it means redoing design and code.
A change reopens signed documents, so change is costly by design.
An unclear requirement blocks every later phase, because no phase starts until the previous one is approved.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call waterfall the linear sequential model or the classic life cycle. Some group waterfall, incremental and spiral as prescriptive process models, because each prescribes when an activity happens.

The incremental model cuts the product into slices called increments, ordered by priority. Each increment passes through all the phases and ends with tested, working software delivered to the user. The first increment is the core; later ones add features on top. Feedback arrives early, so a misread requirement is caught before it spreads through the whole product.

Increments must fit together. The architecture, interfaces and data design have to be settled before increment 1 ships, otherwise increment 3 cannot reuse increment 1's code. Incremental means staged delivery, not absent design.

Evolutionary models assume requirements will move. In prototyping, a quick throwaway version shows the user what the system could be; the reactions sharpen the requirement, and the prototype is then discarded.
The spiral model (Boehm) repeats the phases in loops. Each loop covers one part of the product and has four sectors:

items: Objectives: what this loop must achieve, and its constraints.
Risk analysis: find the biggest risks and cut them, by prototyping the hard part, simulating the load, or buying instead of building.
Engineering: build and test this loop's part of the product.
Evaluation: the customer reviews the result and plans the next loop.

blocks.text: The loop grows wider as its cost grows. Spiral is built for large, risky work: a banking core, a control system, a new platform.

sections.h3: Spiral against incremental, and the Unified Process

blocks.text: Spiral and incremental both deliver in parts. The difference is the risk step. An incremental project can leave risk analysis out; a spiral loop cannot. Remove risk analysis and spiral becomes ordinary iterative development.

The Unified Process (UP) is iterative and incremental, organised in four phases. Inception sets scope, business case and feasibility. Elaboration fixes the architecture baseline and retires the main risks. Construction builds the rest and beta-tests. Transition takes user acceptance and deploys. Each phase holds several iterations, and each iteration is a small full pass through requirements, design, code and test. Architecture gets early attention, which plain incremental often lacks.
A concurrent model draws activities as simultaneous states with events triggering moves. It describes a process rather than planning a delivery, and is mentioned only for completeness.

figure.caption: Waterfall keeps all testing in the final weeks; incremental delivers a tested slice every three weeks; spiral repeats a full loop and adds a risk step each time.

spec.aria: A timeline compares waterfall's single test at the end with incremental releases and repeated spiral loops.

examples.question: A payroll system is delivered in 4 equal increments. Each increment takes 3 weeks to build and 1 week to test. Plan A (waterfall) builds the code for all four increments first, then tests the whole system for 4 weeks, one week per increment. Plan B (incremental) builds and tests each increment before starting the next. Find (a) the week the first tested increment reaches the user under Plan B, (b) the week all testing ends under Plan B, (c) the week building ends under Plan A, (d) the week all testing ends under Plan A.
steps: Length of one incremental cycle = 3 weeks build + 1 week test = 4 weeks.
Increment 1: build weeks 1 to 3, test week 4. First tested increment ready at the end of week 4.
Increment 2: build weeks 5 to 7, test week 8.
Increment 3: build weeks 9 to 11, test week 12.
Increment 4: build weeks 13 to 15, test week 16. Plan B total = 4 increments × 4 weeks = 16 weeks.
Plan A building = 4 increments × 3 weeks = 12 weeks, so weeks 1 to 12.
Plan A testing = 4 increments × 1 week = 4 weeks, so weeks 13 to 16. Plan A total = 12 + 4 = 16 weeks.
Both plans end testing in week 16, but Plan A has no tested software before week 16, while Plan B has a running payroll module from week 4.
A spiral plan would keep the same 16 weeks of engineering but insert risk analysis into each loop, raising effort while lowering the chance of a late surprise.
examples.answer: Incremental delivers its first tested increment at week 4 and ends testing at week 16; waterfall ends building at week 12 and also ends testing at week 16, with nothing tested before then.
examples.check:
increments = 4
build = 3
test = 1
inc_len = build + test
first_ready = inc_len
inc_finish = increments * inc_len
wf_build_end = increments * build
wf_finish = wf_build_end + increments * test
print(first_ready)
print(inc_finish)
print(wf_build_end)
print(wf_finish)

examples.question: A team uses 5 increments. Each takes 2 weeks to build and 1 week to test. Under incremental delivery, when does increment 3 reach the user, and when does all testing end? Under waterfall with the same numbers (build everything, then test one week per increment), when does testing end?
steps: Increment 1 ends week 3, increment 2 ends week 6, increment 3 ends week 9.
All five increments end at 5 × 3 = 15 weeks, so testing ends week 15.
Waterfall building = 5 × 2 = 10 weeks, so weeks 1 to 10.
Waterfall testing = 5 × 1 = 5 weeks, so weeks 11 to 15. Testing ends week 15.
Similar total effort, very different feedback: incremental has a tested slice at week 3.
examples.answer: Increment 3 reaches the user at week 9, incremental testing ends at week 15, and waterfall testing also ends at week 15 with nothing tested before week 11.

traps: Saying spiral is only 'waterfall repeated'. Every loop must contain an explicit risk-analysis step; without it the model is just iterative development.
Calling incremental a form of waterfall. In incremental each increment ends with tested, deliverable software; waterfall tests only after all building is done.
Assuming incremental means no upfront design. The architecture and interfaces must be planned first, or later increments cannot reuse earlier code.
Confusing the four spiral sectors (objectives, risk analysis, engineering, evaluation) with the SDLC phases. The sectors repeat inside every loop.
Confusing UP phases (inception, elaboration, construction, transition) with the SDLC phases. Each UP phase contains several full passes through requirements, design, code and test.

quiz.q: List the four sectors of a spiral loop in the order they occur.
Name the four phases of the Unified Process in order.
Why does waterfall give the user late feedback, even though every phase is reviewed?
quiz.a: Reviews check documents, not running software. The user can execute the product only after building and testing finish, so a requirement error is confirmed late, when fixing it costs a redesign and a rewrite.

quiz.q: A product has 5 increments, each needing 2 weeks to build and 1 week to test. Under incremental delivery, when does increment 3 reach the user and when does testing end?
quiz.a: One increment cycle = 2 + 1 = 3 weeks. Increment 3 ends at 3 × 3 = 9 weeks. All increments end at 5 × 3 = 15 weeks.

quiz.q: Same 5 increments under waterfall: build all code first, then test one week per increment. When does building end and when does testing end?
quiz.a: Building = 5 × 2 = 10 weeks, weeks 1 to 10. Testing = 5 × 1 = 5 weeks, weeks 11 to 15. Testing ends week 15, with no tested software before week 11.

quiz.q: A bank must compute interest exactly as a regulator will define next year, but its mobile app screens are still being debated. Which model suits which part, and why?
quiz.a: The regulated calculation waits for fixed rules, so a document-driven waterfall-style pass after the rules are frozen fits it. The app screens change constantly, so incremental or prototyping fits them. Splitting the work this way keeps a moving requirement from blocking a stable one.

quiz.q: Give two reasons the spiral model suits a large defence system and one reason it is costly for a small team.
quiz.a: It retires the top risks early with prototypes and simulations, and the customer reviews each loop, so a wrong direction is caught before large money is spent. Cost: every loop needs risk analysis, prototyping and a formal review, which a small team cannot afford in time or people.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the pure waterfall survives in fixed-scope contracts and regulated systems, while most product teams run short iterations inside a Scrum or Kanban wrapper (see 1.6). The spiral's risk-first loop reappears in stage-gate reviews for safety-critical systems and in risk-driven architecture work. Process maturity frameworks grade how well an organisation runs a model, not which model it picks. Search for 'Boehm spiral model risk-driven', 'Unified Process phases' and 'iterative and incremental development' for primary descriptions.
